steps.title: Head and body
steps.instruction: Trace the cardinal's head and body, with its pointed crest.

note.text: Feathers cover a bird's body. Soft down feathers underneath trap heat, keeping the bird warm even in winter.
Birds have no teeth. A cardinal's short, very thick beak is strong enough to crack open seeds.

steps.title: Wing
steps.instruction: Trace the wing folded against the body.

note.text: Wings lift a bird into the air. Many birds also have hollow bones, which make them lighter for flying.

steps.title: Wing feathers
steps.instruction: Draw two long flight feathers on the wing.

note.text: Long, stiff flight feathers on the wing push against the air, giving the bird lift and thrust.
The tail helps a bird steer and slow down, a bit like a rudder and brakes together.
Birds rely on sharp eyesight to find food and spot danger.

steps.title: Legs and feet
steps.instruction: Draw both legs and their toes.

note.text: Toes that grip let a cardinal perch on thin branches, even while it sleeps.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: Color the male cardinal's red feathers.

steps.title: Label the parts
steps.instruction: Pick the right name for each numbered part.

targets.role: The pointed feathers on its head.

commonMistakes.Fin: Fins belong to fish. Birds have wings and a tail.
commonMistakes.Teeth: Birds have no teeth: they use their beaks.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why does a cardinal have a short, very thick beak?

options.feedback: Yes. Cardinals split sunflower seeds with their beaks, then use their tongues to take the seed out of the shell.
Fish-catching birds often have long, sharp beaks. A thick beak is built for cracking seeds.
Nectar-sippers like hummingbirds have long, thin beaks.
Wings and feathers help it fly. The beak is for eating.
